title: Power shortages hold back Mexico’s AI data centre push, Bloomberg reports
excerpt: Mexico borders the US but has 71 data centres to Brazil's 225, as grid gaps and slow permits put off AI investors, Bloomberg reports.
content_html:
Mexico is struggling to attract AI data centres because its power grid and permit system cannot keep up, Bloomberg reported. The country borders the US, and data can reach American users almost as fast as from inside the country.

Yet Mexico has 71 of Latin America’s more than 500 data centres, against 225 in Brazil, Bloomberg reported, citing Data Center Map. Chile, a far smaller country, has 66.

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard told Bloomberg that private firms are already building power plants and power lines for some announced projects. He described AI infrastructure as a simple choice for the country.

“There are only two options: Either you have it, or you don’t,” Ebrard told Bloomberg.

Investors describe long delays. CloudHQ, which announced a $4.8bn plan for six data centres in Querétaro last year, said it has applied for about 111 permits, not counting energy ones.

“It takes at least eight months under normal circumstances to get an electricity connection contract,” Luis Lugo, CloudHQ’s top executive in Mexico, told Bloomberg.

Lugo said the process can take up to three years. Meanwhile, President Claudia Sheinbaum plans to add about 32GW of new capacity by 2030. By law, state utility CFE must produce most of it, which Bloomberg said limits private investment.

Mexico also relies heavily on natural gas for power. The government wants 38% of electricity to come from renewables by 2030, up from about a quarter today. Industry group MEXDC says more green power is needed to win over tech firms with climate goals.

Querétaro hosts about 70% of Mexico’s data centres, including sites run by Amazon Web Services and Google. But its grid was not built for such heavy users.

“The Querétaro area is already very saturated,” MEXDC head Juan Carlos Mondragón told Bloomberg.

MEXDC expects just over $20bn in direct investment over the next four years, Bloomberg reported. By contrast, Moody’s estimates US data centre spending will reach $700bn this year.
